intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Pallister-Hall-like syndrome (PHLS) is caused by biallelic mutation in the SMO gene.

checks.claim: Pallister-Hall-like syndrome (PHLS) is caused by biallelic mutation in the SMO gene.
checks.evidence_quote: this is the first report in the literature describing a familial syndrome caused by germline mutations in the Smoothened (SMO) gene
checks.explanation: The abstract supports SMO germline mutations causing the familial syndrome, but does not state that the mutations are biallelic (the full text was not supplied).

paragraphs.text: Pallister-Hall-like syndrome is a developmental disorder characterized by hypothalamic hamartoma and polydactyly. Le et al. (2020) described a wide spectrum of anomalies affecting the brain (hypothalamic hamartoma and microcephaly), the heart (atrioventricular septal defect), the skeleton (postaxial polydactyly, narrow chest, and shortening of long bones), and the enteric nervous system (aganglionosis). Rubino et al. (2019) noted that the disorder differs from Pallister-Hall syndrome, which is autosomal dominant and caused by truncation of GLI3.

checks.evidence_quote: A familial syndrome of hypothalamic hamartomas, polydactyly, and SMO mutations: a clinical report of 2 cases.
checks.explanation: The title describes the syndrome as hypothalamic hamartomas plus polydactyly.

checks.evidence_quote: developmental anomalies affecting the brain (hypothalamic hamartoma and microcephaly)

paragraphs.text: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) reviewed reported cases of Pallister-Hall syndrome and found that only skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities were consistently present. These features resembled the findings in their first 2 cases. They proposed them as the minimum criteria for a distinct, possibly familial entity, and suggested calling it 'congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome' (CHHS).

checks.claim: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) reviewed reported cases of Pallister-Hall syndrome and found that only skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities were consistently present.
checks.evidence_quote: A detailed analysis of the PHS reported cases shows that only skeletal dysplasia and oro-facial abnormalities are present constantly.

checks.claim: The consistently present skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities in reported Pallister-Hall syndrome cases resembled the findings in the first 2 cases of Encha-Razavi et al. (1992).
checks.evidence_quote: They show similarities with those found in our first 2 cases.

checks.claim: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) proposed skeletal dysplasia and orofacial abnormalities as the minimum criteria for a distinct, possibly familial entity.
checks.evidence_quote: These findings prompt us to consider skeletal dysplasia and oro-facial abnormalities as common denominator and minimum criteria required to define a nosologically distinct, possibly familial entity

checks.claim: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) suggested the name 'congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome' (CHHS) for this entity.

paragraphs.text: Encha-Razavi et al. (1992) reported congenital hypothalamic hamartomas found at autopsy in 3 unrelated fetuses. In 2 of the fetuses, the tumor was associated only with skeletal dysplasia. In the third fetus, it was part of a nonrandom association of congenital malformations suggestive of Meckel syndrome. In one family, a previous boy had died soon after birth with similar craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities.

One brother had a large hypothalamic hamartoma that was biopsied and subtotally resected by an endoscopic endonasal approach, and the authors reported its histopathologic findings.

paragraphs.text: Craig et al. (2008) noted that hypothalamic hamartomas are rare, benign congenital tumors associated with intractable epilepsy. Most cases are sporadic and nonsyndromic, and about 5% are associated with Pallister-Hall syndrome. Craig et al. (2008) studied 55 patients with sporadic, nonsyndromic hypothalamic hamartoma and intractable epilepsy, comparing genomic DNA from peripheral blood with DNA from surgically resected hamartoma tissue. Resequencing of GLI3 identified no causative germline mutations. However, they found somatic (tumor-only) chromosomal abnormalities involving the GLI3 locus in 8 of 55 (15%) resected tissue samples. Copy-number analysis on Affymetrix 10K SNP arrays identified a somatic abnormality on chromosome 7p in 1 sample. GLI3 resequencing showed loss of heterozygosity (LOH) within GLI3 in 3 samples, and genotyping of 28 SNPs in and around GLI3 found LOH in 5 more. The authors concluded that these somatic GLI3 abnormalities are associated with the pathogenesis of hypothalamic hamartoma in sporadic, nonsyndromic patients, and noted that the abnormalities appeared highly variable.

They also stated that it was the first familial syndrome other than Pallister-Hall syndrome to be associated with hypothalamic hamartomas.

paragraphs.text: Le et al. (2020) found that cells from individuals with biallelic SMO variants had normal ciliogenesis but severely altered hedgehog signal transduction. This resulted either from altered trafficking at the primary cilium or from abnormal activation of the pathway downstream of SMO. GLI2 accumulated at the ciliary tip independently of hedgehog stimulation. The authors suggested that this points to a role for SMO in regulating basal ciliary trafficking of GLI2 when the pathway is off.
